When you meet Eric Chou in person, one of the first things you notice - long before the technical

not only understands the future of networking, but is determined to help you understand it too.
What Eric has created here is more than a set of recipes. It is a mindset shift.
This book will change how you approach problems, how you build solutions, and how you think
about your relationship with tools - especially AI. For many readers, what follows may be a per-
sonal inflection point. The moment where AI stops being a curiosity or a buzzword and becomes
something far more profound: an extension of your capability as an engineer.

to Python, from CLI mastery to automation frameworks - AI is here to help us build better, faster,
safer networks. Your work quality will rise. Your productivity will surge. Your error rate will drop.
And perhaps most importantly, you will gain something most engineers have never had before: a
domain-aware expert at your side at all times, able to answer questions, explain ideas, generate
examples, and help you think through problems from first principles.
Eric shows you how to use AI correctly - not as a novelty or a magic trick, but as a disciplined
engineering instrument. He goes far beyond “ask ChatGPT for a running configuration,” and in -
stead teaches you how to integrate AI into your daily workflow, your automation pipelines, your
reasoning process, and even the way you design and validate network solutions. By the time you
finish this book, you will not only understand how the tools work, but why they matter - and
why they will become foundational to the next era of network engineering.

98135.content:
1.1 Setting up an OpenAI environment
OpenAI is the dominant player when it comes to Large Language Models (LLMs). The ChatGPT
application was arguably what kick-started the Artificial Intelligence (AI) movement in 2023,
reaching 100 million users in only 2 months. Before we can access OpenAI resources, such as ex-
perimenting with the playground and making API requests, we will need to set up the developer
environment.
In this recipe, we will set up the OpenAI environment to start using OpenAI services, including
generating an API key, familiarizing ourselves with the settings page, and other settings.
Getting ready
We will need to create an OpenAI platform account; this is not the same as an OpenAI account. An
OpenAI account is primarily used for individual users to interact with OpenAI’s AI model through
a web interface such as ChatGPT. An OpenAI platform account, on the other hand, is designed for
developers to build applications and services that leverage OpenAI’s models.
Navigate to https://platform.openai.com/ and sign in to your existing OpenAI account. If you
do not have an account, you can sign up for a free account with an email address. You can also
log in to OpenAI with a valid Google, Microsoft, or Apple account.
Follow the onscreen instructions to complete the creation of your account with the steps of
identity verification and payment setup.

1.2 Experiment with OpenAI LLM models and model
parameters
The OpenAI playground allows the user to select different models and tweak the model param-
eters. The models differ in their capabilities and cost. At the time of writing, here are the general
model types:
• Reasoning models: o-series models that excel at complex, multi-step tasks. Examples:
o4-min, o3-mini, o1-pro.
• Chat models: Original, versatile, high-intelligence models. Examples: GPT-4.1, GPT-4o.
• Cost-optimized models: Smaller, faster models that cost less to run. Examples: o4-mini,
GPT-4.1 mini, GPT-4.1 nana.
• Real-time models: Models capable of real-time text and audio input and outputs.
The pricing of the models can be found at https://platform.openai.com/docs/pricing, in-
crements of price per 1M tokens.
Getting ready
Make sure you are logged in to the OpenAI playground and on the playground interface, as shown
in Figure 1.5.

98142.content:
1.3 Experimenting with OpenAI System message
Located below the parameters is a System message box. By default, there are grayed-out words
stating Describe desired model behavior (tone, tool usage, and response style). This is one of
the first places we can influence how OpenAI interacts with the user by providing desired guide -
lines, tone, and objectives. It is where we can describe the desired model behavior, such as the
tone and response style – for example, answer as if you are a senior network engineer talking to
an intelligent fifth-grader.
Getting ready
Locate the System message box from Figure 1.5 before proceeding with the examples.
How to do it…
1. Let’s begin with the following system message:
You are an AI assistant specialized in network engineering. Your role is
to assist with tasks, provide explanations, and offer guidance related to
network engineering concepts, protocols, tools, and troubleshooting.
The AI LLM Landscape and Key Parameters 12
2. For the user prompt, let’s ask OpenAI What are the steps to set up WiFi 7? and
observe the response.
Figure 1.13 – OpenAI System message
3. Let’s modify the system message to the following:
You are an AI assistant 5th grade teacher specialized in network engineering.
Your role is to assist with tasks, provide explanations, and offer guidance
related to network engineering concepts, protocols, tools, and troubleshooting
and explain them to elementary school kids.
The instructions for the interaction are as follows:
• Provide funny explanations whenever necessary
• Use non-technical language

• Provide the answer in a JSON format

Let’s dive deeper into how it works.
How it works…
The system message can influence the response from OpenAI for the desired output. Here are a
few key concepts for system messages:
• Set the right context: Provide background information or a description of tasks – for
example, “you are an AI assistant specialized in network engineering.”
• Provide clear instructions: Use clear, concise, and unambiguous language and be explicit
about what you want the model to do. For example, “Your role is to assist with tasks, pro-
vide explanations, and offer guidance related to network engineering concepts, protocols,
tools, and troubleshooting and explain them to elementary school kids.”
• Specify output formatting: Specify how you want the output to be structured – for ex-
ample, “... provide the answer in YAML format. ”
There are other prompt engineering methods we will get into in other recipes; this recipe provides
a good start.
There’s more…
OpenAI prompt engineering guide, at https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/text?api-
mode=responses#prompt-engineering, provides excellent guides as a starting point for prompt
engineering for system messages.

Layer 2 of the OSI model is the **Data Link Layer**. It's the layer

between two directly connected nodes – like your computer and your
router – within a local network (like your home or office network).
Here's a breakdown of what it does and its key functions:
**1. Focus:** Reliable data delivery over a physical link.

2.3 Fine-tuning OpenAI responses
The OpenAI LLM base model, sometimes referred to as the foundation model, is amazingly func-
tional and can handle most, if not all, the tasks we throw at it. As we have seen so far, it can help us
with many general network engineering tasks, such as configuring VLANs, assigning IP addresses,
and changing interface descriptions.
But one thing it does not currently do, as no out-of-the-box solution can do, is personalize the
feedback for our specific organizational needs. For example, if our team wants to always use
Loopback 0 for router-id when we configure BGP, the foundation model would not know that.
We can customize our OpenAI model for our specific needs by fine-tuning it. Fine-tuning allows us
to teach OpenAI models our organization’s specific network configuration standard, for example,
so that we do not just get the generic configurations.
In this recipe, we will learn how to prepare training data, execute the fine-tuning process, and
validate results to ensure the model reflects our company’s standardized procedures.
Getting ready

use a Python virtual environment, get an OpenAI API key, and install the openai Python package.

Prompt Engineering for
Reliable Outputs
In the previous two chapters, we saw how we can leverage AI LLMs to answer many questions
and help with daily tasks. By now, we know a big part of working with AI LLMs is how we “ask”
AI for what we need. For example, in Chapter 1, we saw that we received very different responses
when we provided different system messages. This should not come as a surprise to us. After all,
as network engineers, we have spent decades mastering the art of communicating with network
devices through CLI commands. When we open our favorite terminal window and SSH to a router,
we literally open up a “window” of communication to tell the device what we want it to do. In
time, we gradually integrate more communication methods into the device – say, SNMP and API
– but the end goal is still to provide a set of instructions to make the device do what we tell it to do.
Now, with AI LLMs becoming powerful tools in our toolkit, we need to master the way we commu-
nicate with AI models effectively, with prompt engineering. We can think of prompt engineering
as the equivalent of CLI syntax for AI models, except instead of the strict CLI syntax dictated by
the vendor, we use natural language to help AI understand what we need it to do. Just as a poorly
formatted BGP configuration can bring down our network, a poorly crafted prompt can give us
a dangerous AI response.
Often, people think of prompt engineering as a new skill, but it is really about applying existing
network engineering skills to a new type of interface. We need to leverage the same type of sys-
tems thinking and planning from our network engineering background in the new interface to
help the AI model be more effective in solving our problems.
Prompt Engineering for Reliable Outputs 66
In this chapter, we will go over some recipes for constructing effective prompts:
• Giving directions to AI models
• Specifying return formats
• Giving examples
• Providing feedback
• Building prompts gradually
Crafting an effective prompt takes patience and practice – sometimes, we even need to tailor the
prompt toward the specific model we are using. But the recipes covered in this chapter should be
universal, regardless of the model we are using, and provide a good starting point for all queries.
Are you ready? Let’s get started.

3.3 Giving examples
Simply put, the more examples we can provide, the better the AI can understand our needs. In
prompt engineering, concrete examples that we can provide include our organization’s standards,
naming conventions, and best practices.
Let’s consider a newly hired engineer as an example. If we want to have our very capable colleague
configure a router, we would probably get them to reference another similar router, right? “Hey
Bob, take a look at lax-cor-r1 and try to configure lax-cor-r2; they are very similar except for
their loopback interfaces, IP addresses, BGP router-id, and so on.” That is what we mean by
giving examples to AI – we want to give it concrete templates to follow.
Getting ready

3.4 Providing feedback
At the beginning of this chapter, we discussed treating AI as a newly hired, capable-but-new net-
work engineer colleague. Imagine that you have such a colleague on their first day on the job;
do you expect to give them instructions and be done with them? Of course not – not if we are
realistic about producing the right output. Even if we give the colleague detailed instructions
and examples to follow, we would still expect the process to be iterative. We would sometimes
need to repeat important information. The more complex the problem, the more iterative we
expect the process to be.
It would be helpful to review the first set of results produced by the colleague, give feedback based
on the results, and guide them toward the right solution.
In this recipe, we will learn how to use an iterative process to gradually improve AI responses.

3.5 Building prompts gradually
As we stated in the preceding recipe, Providing feedback, the prompt engineering process requires
constant feedback. In some complicated cases, we will need to deliberately build up the prompt
gradually in order to not overwhelm the AI LLM tool. Building complex prompts is similar to de-
signing a complex network or studying for a difficult certification exam, such as CCIE. In terms of
creating a design, we would start with a basic technology that aims for connectivity, satisfy the
basic technical requirements (bandwidth and budget), and then layer it with routing, security,
and monitoring. In terms of studying for an exam, as an example, we would start with the basic
topics, then gradually layer the more advanced technologies on top.
If we try to do too much too fast, with the AI LLM, it often leads to confusion and suboptimal results.
In this recipe, we will learn how to construct prompts systematically, layering complexities grad-
ually until we reach our intended goal.
Getting ready

Chapter 3 93
The key is to realize that AI models are better at doing one thing at a time (just like their human
counterparts) with hierarchical structures.
There’s more…
Once we are comfortable with the separate scripts, we can also combine them into a single script
without losing their hierarchical structure.
The network engineer’s advantage
As with any new technology, one of the most frequently heard questions is, Will this technology
replace my job? I heard this question when network automaton was introduced many years ago:
Will I automate my job away? I also heard a different variation of this question when cloud com-
puting became a mainstay: Will all physical networks become obsolete? However, the question on
everybody’s mind now is, Will AI take away my job?
Many experts predict that the AI revolution is going to be bigger than cloud computing, and
some even argue that it will be bigger than the internet. In that case, it is coming for everyone’s
jobs, not just network engineers’. However, if we consider the previous network automation
and cloud computing example, the network engineer’s role evolves with the new technology;
some functions will be replaced, while other functions will evolve, and some new jobs that we
have not seen before will be introduced. While nobody can foresee the future, I do think network
professionals have a significant advantage, as illustrated by the concepts of prompt engineering
that were introduced in this chapter:
• Network engineering requires breaking down complex problems into logical steps
• Often, network engineers need to specify precise requirements and constraints
• Network engineers need to provide clear examples and documentation
• Network engineering often requires multiple iterations and refined solutions
Do these skills sound familiar? They should, because they are the same skills we discussed in
this chapter that make for good prompts. The same skills that make a good network engineer are
the same that are required for working with AI LLMs when it comes to prompt engineering. The
skills introduced in this chapter are not about replacing your networking knowledge; they are
about amplifying it. As we saw from this chapter’s recipes, providing BGP, VLAN, and security
information significantly improves the time-to-solution with AI’s help.
So, let’s keep our heads up high and learn how to use AI to our advantage!
Prompt Engineering for Reliable Outputs 94
Summary
In this chapter, we learned about the essentials regarding prompt engineering. By using the right
prompt, we can transform AI from a generic helper into a specialized network automation partner
we can all appreciate. Just to recap, we went over giving specific, role-based prompts, specifying
return formats, providing solid examples and feedback, and building prompts gradually in a

step-by-step way.
We should note that prompt engineering is really not a new technology; it involves applying
existing network engineering skills in a new interface – an interface that serves as a gateway to
the AI LLM partner. If we apply the same systematic thinking, precise requirements, and iterative
process that we use for our network engineering skills to working with AI models, we are good to go.
So far in this book, we have mainly been using cloud-based LLMs with API requests. However,
this setup is not always possible in certain environments that require air-gap security or need
to comply with certain government regulations. In the next chapter, we will dive more in-depth
into using local LLMs. See you there!

Network Engineering
In previous chapters, we mostly used cloud-based Large Language Models (LLMs) with API
access to leverage their capabilities. However, there are many reasons why a cloud-based AI LLM
solution might not work in your environment:
• Data sovereignty: In certain industries, such as healthcare, financial, and legal, you may
prefer to house your data, including network information, in your environment, despite
the promise of the provider not to use your data for training.
• Compliance requirements: General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), Health In-
surance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), and Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX)
compliance require air-gapped or on-premises requirements.
• Cost: Pay-per-token cloud solutions might become expensive over time. In comparison,
setting up a local LLM, as introduced in this chapter, does not require ongoing payment
to an AI LLM provider.
• Latency: Cloud-based solutions add route-trip latency and delay to each transaction,

It is worth knowing the origin of LangChain before we start using the tool to put this new ap-
proach into perspective.
What is LangChain all about?
LangChain was created by Harrison Chase in 2022. While working as a Machine Learning (ML)
engineer, he saw how powerful LLMs such as GPT-3 can be, but also that they have their limitations
in that they cannot access up-to-date or proprietary data, interact with external tools, or define
pipelines of workflows. Chase developed LangChain as an open source framework that would
combine LLMs with other components easily and reliably. He called it LangChain by combining
the words “language” and “chains” to illustrate the tool’s objective of combining steps.
LangChain is both an open source project and a business. The business model is similar to Red
Hat and Elastic; the library is free to use, and the company supports development with enterprise
support. This is great for us developers since it is free to learn and experiment with an active
community of support. Once we are ready to put it into production, we can choose to purchase
enterprise support if needed.
Today, LangChain is a core part of the AI developer ecosystem with a vibrant community, third-par-
ty integrations, and funding to accelerate its development.
